results.title: Enraged young protesters take the streets of Europe
results.description: FRANKFURT, Germany — Protesters rallied across Europe on Friday to vent anger over issues from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people. Demonstrators hit the streets in cities from Italy to Germany, Switzerland and Britain, many waving signs emblazoned with “fight for our future,” setting off flares and burning cardboard models of tanks. The rallies, coordinated by a youth-led coalition of over 50 groups, are fueled by grievances that vary from place to place, including Israel’s war in Gaza, high rents and deteriorating learning conditions at schools and universities. But a common theme runs through them — a sense that governments across the continent are too busy with geopolitical crises and helping big business, and not investing enough in the well-being of younger generations. Olivia Ferrario, an 18-year-old high school student at a protest in the Italian city of Milan, told AFP that young people were displaying their “dynamism and determination” by taking to the streets. “If the government does not listen to us, we cannot remain silent,” she said at the demonstration that attracted tens of thousands of protesters. Police were deployed in large numbers due to fears of a repeat of the street violence that has marred recent major protests in France and other countries. ‘Lost so much hope’ In Switzerland, organizers claimed that more than 40,000 protesters had taken to the streets nationwide. “Austerity is social violence,” read a banner in Lausanne, while another blared: “Be vegan, but eat the rich.” The demonstrations were mostly peaceful. But a small number of people clashed with police after it ended, resulting in the deployment of tear gas and water cannon, the domestic Keystone-ATS news agency reported. In Berlin, about 1,000 university students and school pupils protested over concerns including Germany’s rapid rearmament, which has stoked fears of a return to compulsory military service. “I simply think it’s indefensible ... to force someone to learn how to fight and kill, and then send them to war,” Helena Kossatz, 18, who finished high school last year, told AFP. While Europe seeks to rearm in the face of a hostile Russia, organizers of the continent-wide protests say funds allocated to rearmament should be spent on education, youth policies and housing. Several hundred protesters, some in school uniforms, gathered at demonstrations in London outside parliament and in nearby Trafalgar Square, waving placards that said “save higher education” and “Fight for our futures not their wars.” “I’ve lost so much hope,” Eliz, who had taken the day off from college and gave only one name, told AFP. The 18-year-old said she was unsure whether she would go to university, “because of money. Because most jobs are getting taken over by AI. Everyone’s just kind of more depressed.” There were scuffles between groups of right-wing and anti-fascist demonstrators, and AFP saw a handful of arrests. Chants of “Palestine will live forever” rang out at the London protests, and Palestinian flags were on display at several of the demonstrations across Europe. In Rome, high school students marched behind a banner that read: “We will take freedom if no one gives it to us — against the government, the war and the high cost of living.” There were scuffles in the Italian capital, with some protesters throwing bottles and smoke bombs at police. ‘Dreadful’ schools Demonstrators called for more funding for education and railed against increased military spending during protests in the Spanish capital Madrid. Gabriela Gimeno Serrano, a 16-year-old high school student, said there were 33 students in her class with just one teacher. “Classrooms are very small; the facilities are in an absolutely dreadful state,” she told AFP, adding that some schools were even plagued by rats and cockroaches. Protests are set to extend into the weekend, with trade unions and housing associations calling for further demonstrations. The protests come around the anniversary of the Yellow Vests movement in France, which rattled President Emmanuel Macron in 2018 and 2019. Demonstrations are planned there on Saturday.

results.title: Realpolitik of the 49th Asean Summit
results.description: IN international relations, might does not make right. But this is not always the case. Realpolitik is revealed in gatherings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) in the wake of the intensifying rivalry between global superpowers. Realpolitik is a form of statecraft in which countries promote their sovereignty while recognizing the power imbalance and pursuit of respective national interests. Those weaker in resources or military capabilities must work with other nations to hedge against more powerful countries. Realpolitik also challenges Asean centrality. Its founding values of consensus, non-interference, and inclusion are severely tested when powerful countries impose their military and economic leverage on weaker states. But as the world becomes more volatile, Southeast Asian nations are often forced to choose sides. Thinking otherwise is naive and irresponsible in an era of high tariffs, surging oil prices and armed conflicts. Playing both sides, however, could imperil them as they navigate between nuclear powers. In realpolitik, might equals right, taking a cue from 19th-century colonial powers that rode roughshod over smaller countries. Thus, like several of its Southeast Asian neighbors, the Philippines maintains its military alliance with the United States under the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty while diplomatically engaging China, which accounted for 28.6 percent of Philippine imports in 2025. This is called strategic hedging, preserving mutual relations with competing powers without becoming entirely dependent on either. The 49th Asean Summit last week should be realpolitik through diplomacy, brinkmanship and regional consensus. Negotiations on the South China Sea Code of Conduct, however, remained incomplete despite the initial agreement on 80 percent of its provisions. For Myanmar, the slow progress of the Five-Point Consensus revealed Asean’s dilemma of balancing pressure and engagement on a member, given the country’s shared borders with Thailand and Cambodia and other transnational security concerns. The South China Sea dispute remained contentious, particularly with Cambodia and Laos, whose close trade and investment ties with China are undeniable. Meanwhile, Indonesia openly apologized for the transboundary haze that spilled over into Singapore and Malaysia. Realpolitik reached its height during the summit when United States President Donald Trump arrived on the red carpet and was feted at a gala dinner. He commanded the room, reminding Asean leaders who is the big dog in the yard, with the realization that you can’t be on Trump’s bad side. Earlier, leaders of the so-called Quad grouping — composed of the US, India, Japan and Australia — met separately, excluding Southeast Asian nations whose security could nevertheless be affected by their strategic decisions. For the Quad, these nations only played a supporting role, but the reality remains that when conflict erupts, Asean members would be indispensable. The Philippines, however, must remain pragmatic, engaging China as an economic partner while honoring its security commitments to the US. The Philippines is no longer an inconsequential country in regional security. Its gross domestic product in 2025 was estimated by the International Monetary Fund at $500 billion, with a per capita income of over $4,300. Its military has extensive experience fighting communist insurgencies and Muslim rebellions for decades, including urban warfare during the 2017 Marawi City siege. Its military modernization includes BrahMos coastal defense missiles, while American allies have deployed Himars systems, capable of reaching targets at a distance of 250 kilometers. During the 2026 Balikatan exercises, a Tomahawk missile was launched from the southern tip to the northern end of Luzon. In realpolitik, the Philippines is a critical player in regional economic security and geopolitical stability. The proposed first artificial-intelligence (AI) industrial hub in New Clark City under the US-led Pax Silica initiative could reinforce the Philippines’ strategic advantage. However, leftist groups are spreading misinformation about Pax Silica through the backing of Chinese surrogates. The realpolitik is that China dominates 70 percent of the world’s critical earth minerals, which could adversely create bottlenecks in global supply chains. The Philippines shall economically benefit from Pax Silica as a platform to accelerate its AI-based industrial development, attract more investments, and generate more jobs. Pax Silica would diversify supply chains for critical earth minerals, semiconductors and advanced technologies to veer away from excessive dependence on China. Asean members recognize the significance of emerging AI technologies in an increasingly competitive geopolitical landscape. Each nation is recalculating its position to protect its interests while seeking new opportunities for economic rejuvenation. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. successfully steered the 49th Asean Summit at a critical juncture in its history. There are few moments when one genuinely feels proud to be a Filipino. Our nation’s chairmanship demonstrated our leadership in the region. Unfortunately, protests of leftist groups were magnified to overshadow this historic event, reflecting the ill motives of a few who continue to promote a long-rejected ideology. We should unite behind coherent and core strategic priorities rather than be diverted by political rhetoric and inaction. In realpolitik, there are indeed no permanent friends, only permanent national interests. The greatest danger to the Philippines is not that powerful nations will decide our fate, but that our own divisions will allow them to decide it for us.
creator: lloyd c. bautista
